Last time a high-mass star built an iron core, the core collapsed in about a
second, and neutron degeneracy pressure stopped the collapse. This time we look
at what is left: **a neutron star**, a ball of neutrons with more mass than the
Sun and about the size of a city. Nobody expected to see one, because something
so small would be far too faint. Then in 1967 a radio telescope picked up a
signal that ticked like a clock, and the argument that followed showed that it
could only be a spinning neutron star. That argument is the heart of this
lecture. It ends with a question that matters for the rest of the course: how
heavy can a neutron star be before it, too, collapses into a black hole?

## How to read this lecture

**The main reading for this lecture is Kutner, Chapter 11, Sections 11.2,
11.3 and 11.5**, which are in the Canvas Files under *Reading Material*, both
as a PDF and as an accessible Word document. They pick up where last time's
reading stopped. These notes do three jobs. They put neutron stars beside the
white dwarfs of lecture 12, they work through the argument from the pulses to
the neutron star in more detail than Kutner does, and they give you exercises

## Neutron stars and white dwarfs

A neutron star and a white dwarf are the same kind of object at two very
different densities. Each is what is left of a star's core, each has stopped
fusing, and each is held up by degeneracy pressure rather than by heat. The
difference is in which particles do the holding.

| | white dwarf | neutron star |
|:---|:---|:---|
| left by a star of | less than about $8\,M_\odot$ | about 8 to $20\,M_\odot$ |
| mass | up to $1.4\,M_\odot$ | about $1.4\,M_\odot$, and up to about $2\,M_\odot$ |
| radius | about Earth's: Sirius B is $5{,}600\ \mathrm{km}$ | 10 to $15\ \mathrm{km}$, the size of a city |
| average density | about $10^{6}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ | a few times $10^{14}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ |
| held up by | electron degeneracy pressure | neutron degeneracy pressure |

: White dwarfs and neutron stars side by side. The white dwarf column is lecture 12's. {#tbl-compare}

**A neutron star is as dense as an atomic nucleus.** Kutner's Example 11.1
makes the comparison directly: the neutrons are packed nearly as close as they
can go. A neutron star is, in a real sense, one enormous nucleus, held together
by gravity instead of by the nuclear force.

The table also says something less obvious. **Neutron degeneracy pressure is
weaker than electron degeneracy pressure at the same density**, because the
pressure of a degenerate gas goes inversely as the mass of its particles, and a
neutron is about 1,800 times heavier than an electron. So a neutron star can
only hold itself up by being far denser than a white dwarf, which is why the
collapse runs all the way down from thousands of kilometers to tens before it
stops. Kutner works this out in §11.2.1.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-compare}

1. A neutron star has a mass of $2.3\,M_\odot$ and a radius of $11\ \mathrm{km}$.
   How many times denser is it, on average, than lead, which has a density of
   $11.34\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$? What is the escape speed from its surface, as a
   fraction of the speed of light?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   **The question.** What is the average density of a $2.3\,M_\odot$,
   $11\ \mathrm{km}$ neutron star, compared with lead, and how fast must
   something move to escape from its surface?

   First the mass and radius in grams and centimeters, each conversion written
   so that the unwanted unit cancels:

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   M &= 2.3\,M_\odot \times \frac{1.9891 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}{1\,M_\odot}
      \\[0.8em] &= 4.575 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g} , \\[0.8em]
   R &= 11\ \mathrm{km} \times \frac{10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{km}}
      = 1.1 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm} .
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   The density is the mass over the volume of a sphere. Substitute with the
   units attached and no arithmetic yet:

   $$
   \rho = \frac{M}{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3}
        = \frac{4.575 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}
               {\tfrac{4}{3}\pi \left(1.1 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm}\right)^3} .
   $$

   The units are grams over cubic centimeters. *Do the units make sense?* A
   density is a mass per volume, so yes. Now the numbers: the volume is
   $5.58 \times 10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, so

   $$
   \rho = 8.2 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} ,
   $$

   and compared with lead,

   $$
   \frac{\rho}{\rho_{\mathrm{lead}}}
     = \frac{8.2 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}}{11.34\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}}
     = 7.2 \times 10^{13} .
   $$

   The ratio of two densities is a pure number, as it should be. **The neutron
   star is about seventy trillion times denser than lead.**

   For the escape speed, substitute into $v_{\mathrm{esc}} = (2GM/R)^{1/2}$:

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \Bigg( & \frac{2 \times 6.6732 \times 10^{-8}\
       \mathrm{cm^{3}\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}}{1.1 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm}} \\[0.8em]
     & \times 4.575 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g} \Bigg)^{1/2} .
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   Inside the bracket, $\mathrm{cm^{3}\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} \times \mathrm{g} /
   \mathrm{cm} = \mathrm{cm^{2}\,s^{-2}}$, and its square root is
   $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$. *Do the units make sense?* A speed, so yes. Then
   $v_{\mathrm{esc}} = 2.36 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$, and dividing by
   $c = 3.00 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$ gives **0.79**. To leave this
   star you would need to move at nearly 80% of the speed of light.
   :::

2. Use @tbl-compare and the numbers for Sirius B in lecture 12
   ($1.018\,M_\odot$, $0.008098\,R_\odot$) to find how many times denser a
   neutron star of $1.4\,M_\odot$ and $12\ \mathrm{km}$ is than Sirius B, on
   average.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The neutron star's average density is $3.8 \times 10^{14}\
   \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ and Sirius B's is $2.7 \times 10^{6}\
   \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, so the neutron star is about $1.4 \times 10^{8}$ times
   denser.
   :::

:::

## Why the pulses mean a neutron star

In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, a graduate student working with Antony Hewish at
Cambridge, was looking at a radio telescope's paper chart record when she
noticed a signal that did not belong. Looked at closely, it was a train of
sharp pulses, one every $1.337\ \mathrm{s}$, as regular as a clock
[@hewish1968]. Each pulse lasted only about
$0.04\ \mathrm{s}$. The source was half-jokingly named *LGM-1*, for "little
green men", until more were found in other parts of the sky. Today it is called
a **pulsar**, and more than three thousand are known [@manchester2005]. Kutner
tells the story in §11.3.1.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
[The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Hewish, along with Martin Ryle, and
not to Bell. She is now Dame Jocelyn Bell Burnell.]{.aside}
:::

What makes a pulse that regular and that sharp? The argument has two steps, and
each one uses only what we already know.

**The pulse width limits the size.** A source cannot switch on and off faster
than light can cross it. Suppose the whole surface of a star brightened at
once. Light from the near side would reach us first and light from the edges
later, so the pulse we see would be smeared out over the time light takes to
cross the star. A pulse of length $\Delta t$ must therefore come from a region
no bigger than about $c\,\Delta t$. For $0.04\ \mathrm{s}$ that is about
$12{,}000\ \mathrm{km}$, which already rules out any ordinary star. Pulsars
have since been found with pulses a thousandth of a second long, and those come
from regions a few hundred kilometers across at most.

**The period limits the density.** The regularity says that the clock is a
rotation: the star spins, and something on it sweeps past us once a turn.
Kutner explains in §11.3.2 why the other candidates, a star that pulsates or two
stars in orbit, do not work. But a star cannot spin arbitrarily fast. The
material at its equator is moving in a circle, and gravity has to supply the
acceleration that keeps it there, $v^2/r$. If the star spins so fast that
$v^2/r$ is more than gravity can supply, the material flies off and the star
comes apart. So a spinning star of mass $M$ and radius $r$ holds together only
if

$$
\frac{v^2}{r} < \frac{GM}{r^2} ,
$$ {#eq-breakup-condition}

where $v$ is the speed of its equator. Each turn carries the equator once
around the star, so $v = 2\pi r/P$ for a star that spins once every $P$
seconds.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
{{< include ../../in_class/lec14/exercises00.qmd >}}
:::

Putting $v = 2\pi r/P$ into @eq-breakup-condition and dividing the mass by the
volume of the star gives a condition on the star's average density alone:

$$
\rho > \frac{3\pi}{G P^2} .
$$ {#eq-rho-min}

This is a **lower** limit. The faster a star spins, the denser it has to be to
hold itself together, and the mass and the radius do not have to be known
separately. @fig-breakup shows the limit against the period, with real pulsars
on it. Even the first pulsar, at $1.337\ \mathrm{s}$, needs an average density
of about $8 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, about thirty times Sirius B's;
a white dwarf as dense as Sirius B could spin no faster than once every seven
seconds. The Crab pulsar spins about thirty times a second and needs
$10^{11}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, more than any white dwarf can reach. The fastest
pulsar known spins 716 times a second [@hessels2006], and it needs nearly
$10^{14}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. **Only a neutron star is dense enough.**

```{python}
#| label: fig-breakup
#| fig-cap: "The smallest average density a star can have and still hold together, @eq-rho-min, against how fast it spins. Below the line, a star spinning with that period would fly apart. The dots are five real pulsars, on the line at their own periods; the horizontal lines are the average densities of the Sun, of the white dwarf Sirius B and of a typical neutron star. Pulsar periods from the Australia Telescope National Facility's pulsar database [@manchester2005]."
#| fig-alt: "A line chart with logarithmic axes. The horizontal axis is the rotation period in seconds, from one two-thousandth of a second to twenty seconds. The vertical axis is average density in grams per cubic centimeter, from one tenth to ten to the sixteenth. A straight blue line falls from upper left to lower right; the region below it is shaded and labeled the star flies apart. Three dashed horizontal lines are labeled, from bottom to top: the Sun's average density, about 1.4; Sirius B, a white dwarf, about 2.7 million; and a neutron star of 1.4 solar masses and 12 kilometers, about 4 times ten to the fourteenth. Five orange dots sit on the blue line: the first pulsar at 1.34 seconds, Vela at 0.089, the Crab at 0.033, PSR B1937+21 at 0.0016, and the fastest known pulsar at 0.0014 seconds. Every dot lies above the Sirius B line, and the two fastest lie just below the neutron-star line."
#| fig-height: 4.2

G = 6.6732e-8          # cm^3 g^-1 s^-2, the course constants sheet
MSUN, RSUN = 1.9891e33, 6.9598e10

def rho_min(P):
    return 3 * np.pi / (G * P**2)

def mean_density(m_sun, r_cm):
    return m_sun * MSUN / (4 / 3 * np.pi * r_cm**3)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.2))

P = np.logspace(np.log10(5e-4), np.log10(20), 200)
ax.plot(P, rho_min(P), color=BLUE, lw=2, zorder=3)
ax.fill_between(P, 1e-1, rho_min(P), color=BLUE, alpha=0.08, lw=0)
ax.text(0.9, 3e2, "the star flies apart", color=BLUE, fontsize=10,
        ha="center", va="center")

refs = [("the Sun", mean_density(1.0, RSUN)),
        ("Sirius B, a white dwarf", mean_density(1.018, 0.008098 * RSUN)),
        (r"a neutron star, 1.4 $M_\odot$ and 12 km", mean_density(1.4, 12e5))]
# The Sun and Sirius B are labeled at the left, clear of the pulsars; the
# neutron-star line is labeled at the right, clear of the steep part of the curve.
for (label, rho), x, ha in zip(refs, (5e-4, 5e-4, 20), ("left", "left", "right")):
    ax.axhline(rho, color=INK2, lw=0.9, ls="--", zorder=2)
    ax.annotate(label, (x, rho), textcoords="offset points",
                xytext=(4 if ha == "left" else -4, 4),
                ha=ha, va="bottom", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2)

# Periods from the ATNF pulsar database, v2.6.1 (Manchester et al. 2005).
pulsars = [("first pulsar", 1.337302, (8, 4), "left"),
           ("Vela", 0.089328, (8, 4), "left"),
           ("Crab", 0.033392, (8, 4), "left"),
           ("PSR B1937+21", 0.001558, (8, -12), "left"),
           ("fastest known", 0.001396, (8, 4), "left")]
for name, p, off, ha in pulsars:
    ax.plot(p, rho_min(p), "o", color=ORANGE, ms=6, mec=INK, mew=0.5, zorder=4)
    ax.annotate(name, (p, rho_min(p)), textcoords="offset points", xytext=off,
                ha=ha, fontsize=9.5, color=INK)

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(5e-4, 20)
ax.set_ylim(1e-1, 1e16)
ax.set_xlabel(r"rotation period $P$ (s)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"average density $\rho$ (g cm$^{-3}$)")
plt.show()
```

The two steps together rule out everything but a neutron star: the pulse width
says the source is small, and the period says it is dense. A neutron star had
been predicted in the 1930s and then set aside as unobservable. **The pulsars
were the first neutron stars ever seen.**

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-pulses}

1. The first pulsar's pulses last about $0.04\ \mathrm{s}$. How large can the
   region making them be? Compare your answer with the diameter of the Sun
   and with the diameter of Sirius B ($R = 5{,}640\ \mathrm{km}$). Does the
   pulse width alone rule out a white dwarf? What about a pulse $0.001\
   \mathrm{s}$ long?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   About $c \times 0.04\ \mathrm{s} = 12{,}000\ \mathrm{km}$. The Sun is
   $1.4$ million kilometers across, so it is ruled out by a factor of more than
   a hundred. Sirius B is $11{,}300\ \mathrm{km}$ across, just inside the limit,
   so the first pulsar's pulse width alone does **not** rule out a white dwarf;
   it takes the period, @eq-rho-min, to do that. A $0.001\ \mathrm{s}$ pulse
   gives $300\ \mathrm{km}$, which rules out every white dwarf.
   :::

2. Starting from @eq-breakup-condition and $v = 2\pi r/P$, show that a star
   spinning with period $P$ must have an average density greater than
   $3\pi/GP^2$. Then find that density for a star that spins once every
   millisecond.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The density must be more than $1.4 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$,
   about the density of a neutron star.
   :::

:::

## Spinning up and squeezing the field

Kutner's §11.2.2 and §11.2.3 explain why a newborn neutron star should spin
fast and carry a strong magnetic field. Both come from something being
conserved while the core shrinks.

**Spin.** A shrinking core keeps its angular momentum, $J = I\omega$, where
$\omega = 2\pi/P$ and the moment of inertia is $I = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$ for a
uniform sphere. With the mass fixed, $R^2/P$ stays constant, so
$P \propto R^2$: **the period shrinks as the square of the radius.** A core
that collapses from thousands of kilometers to about ten shrinks by a factor of
a hundred or more, so it spins tens of thousands of times faster. It is a
figure skater pulling in their arms, taken to an extreme. Kutner's estimate in
§11.2.2, which starts from the Sun's angular momentum, gives a period of about a
millisecond, close to the fastest a neutron star can spin at all.

**Magnetic field.** The gas in a star conducts electricity so well that the
magnetic field is dragged along with it: the field is *frozen* into the gas,
and the magnetic flux through the star, the field strength times the area,
stays fixed as it shrinks. So

$$
B R^2 = \text{constant} ,
$$ {#eq-flux}

and **the field grows as the square of the shrinkage**, the same factor as the
spin. The fields of most pulsars, worked out from how fast they slow down, are
about $10^{12}$ gauss, a trillion times the Earth's.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-spinup}

1. A main-sequence star of $16\,M_\odot$ has a radius of $10^{6}\ \mathrm{km}$
   and a magnetic field of $100\ \mathrm{G}$ at its magnetic pole. It collapses
   to a neutron star of $2.5\,M_\odot$ and radius $10\ \mathrm{km}$. What is the
   neutron star's field, if the magnetic flux through its surface is conserved?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The field would be $10^{12}\ \mathrm{G}$. The radius shrinks by a factor of $10^{5}$, so the
   field grows by $10^{10}$. The masses do not enter.
   :::

2. Suppose the Sun, which spins once every 25 days, were squeezed to a radius
   of $12\ \mathrm{km}$ without losing any mass or angular momentum, and stayed
   a uniform sphere. What would its period be? Use @eq-rho-min to decide
   whether it would hold together.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   Use $P \propto R^2$, with $R_\odot = 6.9598 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm}$, and
   then compare the average density of $1\,M_\odot$ in a $12\ \mathrm{km}$
   sphere with the smallest density that period allows.

   The period would be $0.64\ \mathrm{ms}$, or about 1,600 turns a second. The
   star's average density would be $2.7 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$,
   less than the $3.4 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ that period needs,
   **so it would fly apart.** A real collapsing core must lose much of its
   angular momentum on the way down, and real pulsars are born spinning more
   slowly than this.
   :::

:::

## The lighthouse, and what keeps the Crab shining

A neutron star does not flash on and off. It shines all the time, in two narrow
beams, and we see a pulse each time a beam sweeps across us, as a ship sees a
lighthouse. Kutner's Fig 11.10 shows the picture. The beams come out along the
**magnetic axis**, which is tilted away from the axis the star spins around,
just as the Earth's magnetic poles are not at its geographic poles. As the star
turns, its enormous magnetic field turns with it, and a moving magnetic field
makes an electric field. Near the surface that electric field is strong enough
to tear charged particles off the star and accelerate them along the field
lines toward the magnetic poles, where they radiate in a narrow beam.

A lighthouse has a consequence. **The beams only sweep out a cone on the sky,
and if the Earth is not on that cone, we never see the pulsar at all.** The
pulsars we know are only the fraction of neutron stars whose beams happen to
cross us.

### Pulsars slow down

The energy in those beams has to come from somewhere, and it comes from the
spin. A spinning star has kinetic energy $E = \tfrac12 I\omega^2$, which with
$\omega = 2\pi/P$ is $E = 2\pi^2 I/P^2$. Every pulsar is slowing down, so its
period grows a little every second, at a rate we write $\dot P$. Differentiating
$E$ gives the rate at which the star loses its spin energy,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\,\frac{4\pi^2 I\,\dot P}{P^3} .
$$ {#eq-spindown}

Kutner reaches the same result in another form, his equation 11.15, and uses it
in Example 11.4. The minus sign says the energy is decreasing. The rate
$\dot P$ is a tiny number, a time per time, so it has no units.

Lecture 13 ended with a puzzle. The Crab Nebula shines in synchrotron light,
which needs electrons moving close to the speed of light, and those electrons
should have lost their energy long ago. Yet the nebula still shines, nearly a
thousand years after the supernova. **At its center is a pulsar**, the bright
spot in @fig-crab, and @eq-spindown tells us whether it can be the power
supply.

![The Crab Nebula, the remnant of the supernova seen in 1054, in a composite of an X-ray image from the Chandra X-ray Observatory (blue) and a visible-light image from the Hubble Space Telescope (red). The pulsar is the bright point near the center. The rings and jets around it, seen in X-rays, are where its outflow of particles meets the nebula. Credit: X-ray, NASA/CXC/ASU/J. Hester et al.; optical, NASA/HST/ASU/J. Hester et al. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Chandra-crab.jpg).](crab-chandra-hubble.jpg){#fig-crab fig-alt="A square color image of a glowing cloud on a black, star-speckled background. Red and magenta wisps of gas fill most of the frame. In the middle is a paler blue-white haze, and near its center a bright point of light sits inside a set of faint, tilted, nested rings, with a fainter streak extending from it. A few stars with spikes of light are scattered over the image."}

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: the power of the Crab pulsar"}
**The question.** The Crab pulsar spins once every $P = 0.0334\ \mathrm{s}$
and slows down at $\dot P = 4.21 \times 10^{-13}$ [@manchester2005]. Taking a
moment of inertia of $I = 10^{45}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^2}$, typical for a neutron
star, at what rate is it losing its spin energy? Is that enough to keep the
nebula shining, which Kutner puts at about $3 \times 10^{38}\
\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$?

Substitute into @eq-spindown with the units attached, leaving out the minus
sign since we want the rate of loss:

$$
\left| \frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} \right|
  = \frac{4\pi^2 \times 10^{45}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^2} \times 4.21 \times 10^{-13}}
         {\left(0.0334\ \mathrm{s}\right)^3} .
$$

Before any arithmetic, the units: $\dot P$ has none, so we have
$\mathrm{g\,cm^2} / \mathrm{s^3} = \mathrm{g\,cm^2\,s^{-2}} \times
\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, which is ergs per second. *Do the units make sense?* We want a
rate of energy loss, a power, so yes. Now the numbers. The bottom is
$3.72 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s^3}$, so

$$
\left| \frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} \right|
  = 4.5 \times 10^{38}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}} ,
$$

about a hundred thousand times the luminosity of the Sun. **That is more than
the nebula gives off**, so the slowing pulsar can pay for all of it, with some
to spare. The slow-down of one star twenty kilometers across powers a nebula
about ten light-years across.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-spindown}

1. The Crab pulsar's spin energy is $E = 2\pi^2 I/P^2$. Use the numbers in the
   worked example to find how long it would take to lose all of that energy at
   today's rate, $E \big/ |\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t|$. Kutner calls this the
   pulsar's lifetime in Example 11.4. Compare it with the time since the
   supernova was seen, in 1054.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The spin energy is $E = 1.8 \times 10^{49}\ \mathrm{erg}$, and dividing by
   $4.5 \times 10^{38}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ gives $4.0 \times 10^{10}\
   \mathrm{s}$, about 1,260 years. Algebraically it is just $P/2\dot P$. The
   supernova was seen 972 years ago, so the two agree to within about 30%. The
   number is a useful estimate of a pulsar's age, and astronomers call it the
   *characteristic age*.
   :::

2. Explain why there must be many more neutron stars in our galaxy than the
   pulsars that have been found, even counting only the ones close enough to
   detect.

:::

## How heavy can a neutron star be?

Neutron degeneracy pressure has a limit, just as electron degeneracy pressure
does, and for the same reason: pile on enough mass and the particles are
squeezed until they move close to the speed of light, and then the pressure
cannot keep up with gravity. Above that mass, **no pressure we know of can hold
the star up.** It collapses past its own Schwarzschild radius and becomes a
black hole, the object of the first half of this course, now made by an
ordinary dying star.

A neutron star is already not far from that edge. A $1.4\,M_\odot$ neutron
star has a Schwarzschild radius of about $4\ \mathrm{km}$, a third of its radius,
so it is the most compact object we know of that is not a black hole.

::: {.callout-warning .textbook-watch title="Textbook watch (Kutner): the maximum mass of a neutron star is lower than §11.5 says"}
Kutner gives the largest mass of a neutron star as about $3\,M_\odot$, and
perhaps as much as $8\,M_\odot$. Measurements made since point lower. One of
the heaviest neutron stars with a precisely measured mass, the pulsar
PSR J0740+6620, is $2.08 \pm 0.07\,M_\odot$ [@fonseca2021], so the maximum is
at least that. The merging neutron stars of GW170817, from lecture 10, have
been used to argue that it is not much more, about $2.2\,M_\odot$
[@margalit2017]. The exact number is still debated, but **the maximum mass of a
neutron star is now thought to be a little above $2\,M_\odot$**, not 3 and
certainly not 8.
:::

## If you want to go further

None of this section is needed for what comes before or after.

**Inside a neutron star.** Kutner's Fig 11.7 shows the structure: a solid crust
about a kilometer thick, made of nuclei such as iron, over an interior of
neutrons that flow without any friction, a **superfluid**. The atmosphere above
the crust is about a centimeter thick.

**Glitches.** Every so often a pulsar suddenly speeds up a little and then goes
on slowing down. Kutner's Fig 11.12 marks them for the Crab. One explanation is
a starquake: the crust cracks, settles a fraction of a centimeter smaller and,
keeping its angular momentum, spins faster. Kutner works out how small a change
it takes in Example 11.5.

**Pulsars as probes.** A radio pulse travels through the thin gas between the
stars, and its free electrons slow the longer wavelengths more than the shorter
ones. So each pulse arrives a little later at long wavelengths than at short
ones, and the delay measures how much gas the pulse crossed. That is Kutner's
§11.4.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## Summary

| idea | result | why it matters |
|:---|:---|:---|
| A neutron star | about $1.4\,M_\odot$ in a sphere 10 to $15\ \mathrm{km}$ across, as dense as a nucleus | the second compact object, held up by neutron degeneracy pressure |
| The pulse width | a pulse of length $\Delta t$ comes from a region no larger than $c\,\Delta t$ | the source is small |
| The period | a star spinning with period $P$ needs $\rho > 3\pi/GP^2$ | only a neutron star is dense enough for the pulsars |
| Spin-up and flux freezing | $P \propto R^2$ and $B \propto 1/R^2$ as the core shrinks | why pulsars spin fast and have fields of about $10^{12}\ \mathrm{G}$ |
| Spin-down | $\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t = -4\pi^2 I\dot P/P^3$ | the Crab pulsar powers the Crab Nebula |
| The maximum mass | a little above $2\,M_\odot$ | anything heavier left by a collapse is a black hole |

A white dwarf is held up by electrons and a neutron star by neutrons. Above a
little more than two solar masses, nothing is left to do the job, and the
course arrives at its subject: a black hole made by a star. A lone black hole
gives off no light, though, so finding one takes a companion. Next time we look
at stars in close pairs, where one star can feed gas to a white dwarf, a
neutron star or a black hole, and the gas lights up as it falls.
